The story is rich with subtext that naturally enhances both the physical setting and the emotional landscape of the characters without feeling forced. 

For example, the setting of the coastal Maine beach at low tide operates on both a surface and subtextual level. On the surface, Arthur and Clara are looking at a granite island and realizing they cannot walk out to it because the tide is coming in. Subtextually, the disappearing sandbar and the encroaching tide mirror the ticking clock of their twenty-eight-day residency. When the tide later creeps into their hollow in the dunes and sets Clara’s sandal afloat, it serves as a subtle, physical manifestation of their "biosphere" collapsing as reality and their normal lives rush back in. 

Furthermore, the final scene in the broken-down Volvo uses the immediate setting and dialogue to convey deep subtext. As the car windows fog up, creating a "pearl-grey blindness that erased the ocean and the road back," it symbolizes their brief, desperate attempt to suspend time and block out their impending separation. Within this enclosed setting, Arthur tells Clara about 1890s Chicago bathhouses—how the city gave laborers twenty minutes to wash in hopes it would cure their anarchism, only to end up with "cleaner anarchists." On the surface, he is just sharing his academic research. The subtext, however, is a poignant reflection on their own situation: the idyllic artist colony gave them a temporary respite (their "twenty minutes"), but it hasn't fundamentally changed who they are or fixed the discontent in the lives they must return to tomorrow. When the dying battery finally extinguishes the dome light as the tide erases their footprints outside, the setting seamlessly underscores the quiet, inevitable end of their fleeting romance.
